title: Moral Luck
objective: After this level you can explain Bernard Williams’s and Thomas Nagel’s puzzle of moral luck, using two equally careless drivers with different outcomes.
summary: Williams and Nagel showed that our blame depends on luck, clashing with the Control Principle; some deny moral luck by locating blame in intentions, and Nagel replied that luck reaches intentions too.

cards.headline: Two drivers make the same mistake. Only one of them is unlucky.
cards.body: Should we blame them differently? Most of us do. Two philosophers asked whether we should.

cards.headline: A phrase that shouldn’t work
cards.body: In 1976 Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel published a now classic pair of papers, both called “Moral Luck”. Williams expected the phrase to sound like an oxymoron. Morality is supposed to be the part of life luck can’t reach. Kant wrote that a good will, even if it achieved nothing, would still shine like a jewel by itself.

cards.headline: The Control Principle
cards.body: Here’s a principle most people find compelling: you are morally assessable only for what depends on factors under your control. If someone steps on your toes because she was pushed, the urge to blame her evaporates. It follows that two people who differ only in factors beyond their control shouldn’t be judged differently.

cards.headline: Two careless drivers
cards.body: Now take two otherwise careful drivers who both forgot to have their brakes checked. Both brakes fail. Only one finds a child in the path of the car. Their carelessness was identical; only the outcome differed. Judge them differently and you clash with the Control Principle. Nagel identified four kinds of moral luck, and this one is now called resultant luck: luck in how things turn out.

mascot.line: Keep this: same carelessness, different outcome. The whole puzzle lives in that gap.

cards.headline: Deny it, or accept it?
cards.body: Some deny that luck changes what anyone deserves. Adam Smith held that all praise and blame ultimately belong to the intention of the heart, and many philosophers say luck changes only how clearly we can see someone’s fault. Nagel replied that luck shapes our intentions too, through circumstances and character, so retreating inward doesn’t escape it.

questions.prompt: Of Nagel’s kinds of moral luck, luck in how things turn out is _____ luck.

options.label: constitutive
options.rationale: That is luck in who you are.

options.label: circumstantial
options.rationale: That is luck in the situation you face.

options.label: causal
options.rationale: That concerns how you are shaped by prior causes.

questions.explanation: Resultant luck is luck in how things turn out, as with the two drivers.

questions.prompt: Two people send the same unkind message, but only one recipient happens to read it. On the reply that denies moral luck, what has luck changed?

options.label: How much each person deserves to be blamed
options.rationale: The reply denies that luck changes desert.

options.label: Only how clearly we can see each person’s fault
Which person had control over the message

questions.explanation: Those who deny moral luck say luck changes only how visible someone’s fault is, not the fault itself.

questions.prompt: Match each thinker with the idea linked to him.
questions.explanation: Williams expected “moral luck” to sound like an oxymoron, Nagel identified four kinds of moral luck, Kant said a good will would shine like a jewel, and Adam Smith tied praise and blame to the intention of the heart.
